newsitem.title: UK: Scottish seat is challenge for UK's Labour.
newsitem.headline: Scottish seat is challenge for UK's Labour.

text.p: Tony Blair's Labour party may be sweeping all before it in national British opinion polls but it has a challenge on its hands in a corner of northeast Scotland.

It was in Inverness, where Labour's Scottish party held its annual conference this weekend, that Blair scored a decisive victory over left-wing diehards in 1995 when he won approval to scrap Labour's dog-eared Marxist constitution.
He has now carved out a commanding poll lead that suggests he will end Labour's 18 years in opposition at the forthcoming general election, which will probably be held on May 1.

But the politics of Scotland, skewed by geography, history, class and factionalism, mean Blair cannot take for granted that Labour will add much to its current tally of 49 Scottish seats out of a total of 72.
The seat of Inverness East, Nairn and Lochaber, which contains some of Britain's most majestic highland scenery, is a case in point.

In the 1992 election, it was Britain's only four-way marginal contest. Sir Russell Johnston, who is now retiring, retained the seat for the centre-left Liberal Democrats with just 26 percent of the vote.
Labour came second with 25.1 percent, followed by the Scottish Nationalist Party (SNP) with 24.7 percent and the ruling Conservatives with 22.6 percent.

Subsequent boundary changes mean Labour probably has more ground to make up and the party's Scottish high command is pulling out all the stops to capture what it identifies as one of Scotalnd's seven key marginal seats.

"We have only one single objective between now and polling day -- and that is to mobilise our vote, increase our share of the vote, win new seats and form a Labour government," said Henry McLeish, a fast-rising member of parliament who is coordinating Labour's Scottish campaign.
The biggest challenge to Labour candidate David Stewart could come from the SNP, which has four seats in Scotland to 10 for the Conservatives and nine for the Liberal Democrats.

Dismissed by its bigger brethren as a single-issue pressure group, the pro-independence party is making Labour squirm by loudly advocating higher taxes to improve hard-pressed public services -- a message that goes down much better in Scotland than in England.

SNP leader Alex Salmond tried to spoil Labour's conference by saying its policy pledges entailed so little extra public spending that Blair had cloned Labour from Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives.
"The SNP and independence are the only alternative to the 'Blajor' politics of Middle England," said the SNP's candidate for Inverness East, Fergus Ewing.

The local consensus is that the Liberal Democrats will lose the seat because the personal loyalty Johnston built up over 33 years in parliament will not pass to his young would-be successor, Stephen Gallagher.
Gallagher, not surprisingly, disagrees. He is also attacking Labour for its timid spending plans -- the Lib Dems would raise income tax to pay for better schools.
About the only thing on which Labour, the SNP and the Lib Dems would agree is that support for the Conservative candidate, Mary Scanlon, is crumbling.

"I would vigorously state the opposite," retorts Scanlon, who says the government's economic policies have given Inverness below-average unemployment and made it one of the fastest-growing areas of Britain.
